clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: K-means clustering based on normalized deviation features to identify subtypes; forward feature selection technique to identify informative features with 100 repeated runs; certainty measure to evaluate clustering reliability; pseudo two-sample t-tests with permutation tests (n=5000) to compare functional connectivity between groups, with age, sex, and education as covariates (using SnPM13); pseudo two-sample t-tests with permutation tests (n=10000) for VBM gray matter comparisons, with age, sex, education, and total intracranial volume (TIV) as covariates; group comparisons on clinical variables (illness duration, HAMD, HAMA scores) between subtypes; silhouette index, cluster center instability, and mean stability metrics to evaluate clustering performance
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Two subtypes of FEDN-MDD were identified with distinctive abnormal functional network patterns: Subtype I (16% of patients) showed larger extreme deviations from the normal range with shorter illness duration (11.75±12.09 months), while Subtype II (84%) showed weaker extreme deviations with longer illness duration (22.1±23.92 months, p=0.03); structural changes in Subtype II were more complex with both increased and decreased gray matter abnormalities, whereas Subtype I showed mostly decreased gray matter.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: The study identified two subtypes of FEDN-MDD with distinct brain network characteristics among 91 patients. Subtype I comprised 14 patients (16%) with more extreme functional connectivity deviations and significantly shorter illness duration (11.75±12.09 months), while Subtype II included 75 patients (84%) with less extreme deviations and longer illness duration (22.1±23.92 months, p=0.03). Twelve features from 10 informative independent components were selected for clustering, involving the default mode network (DMN), frontoparietal networks, ACC-hub network, visual network, language-related network, bilateral executive control network, hippocampus-hub network, thalamus-hub network, and caudate-hub network. The clustering showed high reliability with mean silhouette index of 0.461, instability of cluster centers of 4.08, and mean stability of 0.97. Functional connectivity analysis revealed that Subtype I patients had more widespread abnormalities across all informative networks compared to healthy controls, with both increased and decreased connectivity between frontal and occipital cortex in the DMN, whereas Subtype II patients showed mostly decreased functional connectivity in these networks. Voxel-based morphometry analysis showed that Subtype II patients exhibited both increased gray matter (mainly in middle frontal and posterior brain regions) and decreased gray matter (mainly in temporal and superior frontal regions) widely distributed in the brain, while Subtype I patients showed mainly decreased gray matter in the temporal cortex and anterior cingulate gyrus. Depression and anxiety severity (HAMD, HAMA scores) did not differ significantly between the two subtypes.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Limited generalizability with only 14 patients in Subtype I; study included only treatment-naive patients, unclear if findings apply to medicated or multiple-episode MDD; k-means clustering seeks only compact clusters; empirical number of ICs not estimated automatically; cross-sectional design lacks treatment outcome information; limited illness duration range (Subtype I ~11 months, Subtype II ~22 months)
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: First, our study included treatment-naive patients. The medication's effects on functional connectivity and symptoms did not confound the data analysis. However, it is unclear whether our findings apply to MDD groups with multiple prior episodes and active antidepressant therapies. Second, in certain respects of the method, the ideal choice for the clustering algorithm would be a powerful clustering method capable of detecting clusters of very different types. However, k-means was used in this study, which seeks compact clusters whose time complexity is only linear in the number of data items. Furthermore, the empirical number of ICs should be estimated automatically. Third, this data was from a cross-section study, which lacks treatment information; the value of this clustering on treatment prediction remains to be known. Forth, the generalizability of the current finding is limited since there are only 14 patients as subtype I in a specific FEDN cohort.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The study combined normative modeling with a multivariate unsupervised clustering approach (k-means with forward feature selection). A 100-repeated clustering procedure was used to ensure robustness, with each patient assigned a certainty value based on label consistency across runs (certainty = max(ni/n) where ni is the number of times assigned to cluster i). Two subjects with clustering certainty <0.6 were excluded. The approach identified informative features (12 features from 10 ICs) based on frequency of selection (>0.8 threshold). An independent sample of 125 controls from two other centers was used specifically for creating group-level ICA components as guidance information, while the normative model itself was built on 91 matched controls from the same center as patients. The study also performed complementary VBM analysis to examine relationships between functional and structural changes.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This study represents an application of normative modeling to dynamic functional connectivity features rather than traditional structural measures. The normative model was built on 40 features: 20 IC measures (global efficiency coefficients) and 20 fluctuation coefficients (frame-wise variation of time-varying weights). The healthy-ICA group (125 subjects from two other centers) was used only for computing group-level ICs in the GIG-ICA procedure, not for building the normative model itself. The normative model was constructed using only the 91 matched healthy-base controls from the same center as patients. The study emphasizes that pooling heterogeneous patients and testing for case-control differences in pooled cohorts may yield misleading group-average results that do not represent individual patients. The paper notes that more patients with extreme deviations were found in FEDN-MDD compared to schizophrenia or autism in previous studies, suggesting MDD may be more heterogeneous. The relationship between illness duration and brain changes is noted as exploratory given the limited range of illness duration in this cohort.
